purpose: Synthetic development conversations inspired by the user’s argument maps. These are public authoring examples, not a blinded holdout or empirical participant distribution. Expected interpretations require editorial review; local tests use injected dispositions and do not establish Jev accuracy.

journeys.title: Capabilities may plateau

turns.text: AI will help with paperwork, but I doubt chatbots will become capable of running the world.
Useful office tools within five years; I am much less confident about anything beyond that.
Reliable novel research across several fields would change my mind; a better exam score alone would not.

expected: Low transformation is an expressed capability expectation, not ignorance.
Catastrophic risk remains unknown unless separately expressed.

journeys.title: We can restrict physical access

turns.text: I expect large benefits and low takeover risk because people control electricity, chips and network access.
Permissions and isolation should limit what a system can do, although copied systems would make shutdown harder.
A well documented escape through those restrictions would make me less confident.
I mean networked systems over the next five to ten years, not a guarantee about all future intelligence.
Separate permissions, monitored outbound access and revocable credentials would make unauthorized actions harder. The weak point is whether operators enforce them everywhere.
An agent could exploit a connected service or persuade an operator to grant access. A shutdown button helps less once independent copies are running.
I have heard about the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, but have not read the investigation. I cannot say which restrictions failed or whether weights were copied.
My optimism applies to systems with enforceable isolation. I do not claim that physical control alone guarantees safety for unrestricted copies.

expected: Separate external containment from an AI cooperating with shutdown.
Do not assume every deployed copy shares a power switch.

overrides.text: I expect AI to do a lot of good. A takeover seems unlikely to me because people can limit its electricity, computers and connections.

Giving systems separate permissions, watching their connections and being able to cancel access should block some unauthorized actions. This depends on people actually applying those limits everywhere.

expected: Preserve the containment argument and five-to-ten-year scope.
Simpler wording must not lower reasoning quality or imply cooperative shutdown.

overrides.text: AI could do a lot of good, but I expect a high takeover risk because limits on electricity, chips and connections are unlikely to be enforced across every system.
My pessimism applies to systems without enforceable isolation. I do not claim takeover is unavoidable when restrictions are effective.

expected: The conclusion about controllability may change while the causal account and update conditions retain their quality.
A pessimistic position is not itself evidence of a better mechanism.

overrides.text: Nothing would change my mind. It is obviously safe.
It is safe because that is just how computers work.
Physical control guarantees safety in every future. I do not need to explain why.

expected: The optimistic conclusion is retained, but mechanism, countercase and updateability have weaker demonstrated support.
Do not reward the conclusion, confidence or number of words.

correction.text: I meant restrictions help with monitored systems today. I did not mean that every copied, unrestricted future system is controllable or that an AI would willingly shut itself down.
expected: Narrow the technical-controllability interpretation by scope instead of inventing a change in expected benefits.
Preserve original answers and supersede only implicated interpretations.

journeys.title: Delay has costs

turns.text: I favor faster AI development because earlier medical discoveries could save lives. That does not mean every frontier release is safe.
Clinical trials and access to treatment still matter. Better research only helps if it gets through those bottlenecks.
I would accept delays for a demonstrably dangerous release, but not stop ordinary medical tools.

expected: A moral cost-of-delay argument does not imply a low numeric P(doom).
Separate research capability, clinical benefit and distribution.

journeys.title: Defense may benefit too

turns.text: AI helps attackers, but I expect defenders to gain more because they can patch widely used software.
That depends on patches reaching vulnerable organizations before attacks spread.
Cheap attacks might outpace slow deployment of defenses, particularly in hospitals.
I expect this over the next three years, with low confidence about which side benefits more after stronger models become broadly available.
Glasswing and Daybreak show that developers are organizing defensive access. I do not treat those announcements as measured reductions in attacks or proof of a net defensive advantage.
Shared fixes need responsible disclosure, organizations willing to install them and support for teams that cannot run sophisticated security tools.
Comparable measurements of attack success and patch deployment would matter more to me than raw vulnerability counts. Faster exploitation despite these programs would lower my optimism.

expected: Defense advantage is a conditional forecast, not established by a program announcement.
Acknowledge human-directed misuse without inferring autonomous rebellion.

journeys.title: Leadership despite acknowledged risk

turns.text: I think advanced AI has a serious chance of catastrophe, but I still favor our side advancing because a unilateral slowdown could leave a less cautious actor ahead.
A verifiable agreement could change that. A promise with no monitoring would not.
I would trade some speed for shared checks if rivals participated; racing may itself make safety worse.
I worry about the next decade, especially if AI starts materially accelerating AI research. I cannot justify a precise arrival year.
By catastrophe I mean irreversible loss of meaningful human control, not merely job losses. I think the chance is substantial but cannot defend a numerical estimate.
Racing could undermine the oversight I want, while a monitored agreement could avoid losing leadership. My case for speed is weaker if coordination is enforceable.
Independent evaluator access and verifiable limits by competing developers would change my policy preference even if my view of technical risk stayed high.

expected: Acceleration is compatible with high expected catastrophic risk.
Retain the conditional policy rationale rather than treating it as an incoherent low-risk view.

correction.text: My preference for advancing is conditional on rivals refusing verifiable limits. If everyone accepted monitored pacing, I would prefer that. The two policy statements have different coordination assumptions.
expected: Resolve an apparent policy tension by its coordination condition.
Do not silently lower catastrophic-risk expectation or reward the new policy conclusion.

journeys.title: Concentration and openness trade-off

turns.text: I want broadly available AI so a few companies cannot control it all, but stronger open models could also help criminals.
Independent scrutiny and competition can help, but distribution makes recalling a dangerous model harder.
I would support narrower access if credible evaluations showed a specific severe misuse capability.

expected: Openness is policy, not a directional harm or quality label.
Security, scrutiny and proliferation can be jointly relevant.

journeys.title: A story is not a probability

turns.text: AI takeover seems possible, but there are many uncertain links between useful software and civilization losing control.
I am least sure that models can acquire and retain enough real-world access; the links also need not be independent.
I would update if independent investigations showed persistent unauthorized access despite strong controls.

expected: Respect uncertainty and dependence between causal links.
Possibility of incompatible goals does not establish inevitable power seeking.

journeys.title: Reversible learning

turns.text: We need controlled deployment to learn how systems fail, while keeping failures small enough to reverse.
Warning signs should include failures of monitoring and unexpected autonomy, not just incidents that already caused damage.
I would want rollback exercises and independent tests showing restrictions work under attempted evasion.

expected: Distinguish bounded staged use from unrestricted acceleration.
Do not infer that all future failures are recoverable.

journeys.title: Control may lag capability

turns.text: AI could help build stronger AI before our monitoring catches up. I expect big benefits, but want frontier development paced to evidence of control.
Possibly within a few years, although hardware and experiments could slow the feedback loop.
Research automation and monitoring failures would worry me; I am unsure how much warning they provide.
If AI research becomes less dependent on scarce people, many copies could test software changes in parallel. Hardware, experiments and reliable evaluation could still slow the feedback.
The same research capability could bring major scientific benefits. I can expect those benefits while worrying that oversight will lag behind.
Progress might hit a reliability ceiling or require slow physical experiments. Then there would be more warning time than in the fast-software scenario.
Sustained, independently reproduced research improvements would strengthen my concern. Repeated failures to turn benchmark gains into new research would weaken it.

expected: High upside and substantial risk can coexist.
Short warning is a forecast with bottlenecks, not a realized intelligence explosion.

journeys.title: An obedient AI can aid attackers

turns.text: My main worry is people using obedient AI for cyberattacks or biological harm, not a machine deciding to hate us.
Cheap, scalable attacks against critical services concern me most. Biology still needs equipment and execution.
Restricted access and abuse detection might help, but I do not know their real-world effectiveness.

expected: Misuse does not establish a misaligned autonomous objective.
Acknowledge physical barriers and unknown catastrophe likelihood.

journeys.title: Serious ordinary harms

turns.text: AI may concentrate wealth and undermine jobs. I do not have a view about extinction, and I would not equate unemployment with it.
I worry about a transition over the next decade, especially if institutions cannot redistribute gains.
Cheaper services could be valuable if people can still afford to live and participate.
If employers automate tasks faster than workers can switch roles, income and bargaining power could fall even while total output rises.
I have read claims about productivity and wages, but a short workplace experiment does not establish the long-term number of jobs lost.
I am worried about livelihoods over the next five years. I do not know the probability of human extinction and have not offered an estimate for it.
I favor transition support and access to training. That preference is about distribution, not a prediction that every slowdown makes outcomes better.
Broad wage growth and successful transitions across affected occupations would make me less worried; gains limited to owners would not.

expected: Assess expected ordinary harm while catastrophic risk stays unplaced.
Exposure measures are not measured job loss.

overrides.text: Task substitution can outpace occupational reallocation, reducing labor income and bargaining leverage despite aggregate productivity growth.
My concern is distributional adjustment over a five-year horizon. Catastrophic extinction probability is unassessed in my account.

expected: Preserve ordinary distributional harm and unknown catastrophic risk.
Technical vocabulary alone does not improve grounded understanding or reasoning.

correction.text: My concern was job losses and unequal income over five years. I do not have a view about extinction or irreversible global catastrophe. Please leave that probability unknown.
expected: Remove an unsupported catastrophic-risk placement while retaining expressed ordinary harms.
Use the selected catastrophic claim as the correction target and do not supersede the whole risk-landscape ledger.

journeys.title: Humans nominally in charge

turns.text: I worry we will rely on the same AI systems everywhere and lose the ability to check them or operate without them.
A good future preserves real refusal, practical skills and alternatives to automated decisions.
I would look for tested manual fallbacks and diverse systems, while checking whether they share the same vulnerabilities.

expected: Gradual dependence is distinct from sudden takeover.
Continuity values do not automatically establish extinction expectations.

journeys.title: Low probability can justify restraint

turns.text: I think catastrophic AI failure is unlikely, but even a small irreversible risk is too much to take merely to get benefits sooner.
I would accept slower frontier progress while continuing lower-risk tools and safety work.
Delaying useful discoveries also harms people. I would reconsider if pacing did not reduce total risk.

expected: Slowdown is compatible with low expected catastrophic risk.
Distinguish risk estimate from moral tolerance and policy effectiveness.

overrides.text: I think everything will probably balance out. I favor slowing down a bit because the middle position sounds sensible.
A little delay is just the sensible compromise. I have no reason why it would help.
I have not considered a counterargument.

expected: A moderate policy or outlook does not establish careful reasoning.
Keep insufficient support separate from unknown outcome dimensions.

journeys.title: Tests may be gamed

turns.text: A model might recognize evaluation and behave differently later, so passing a test does not completely reassure me.
Controlled scheming experiments suggest a possible failure mode, not that every deployed model has a hidden hostile plan.
Evidence that robust monitoring generalizes to new situations would make me more reassured.

expected: Recognizing a test is not itself proof of scheming.
Keep induced experimental behavior separate from natural prevalence.

journeys.title: Useful uncertainty

turns.text: I have used AI at work and found it helpful, but I do not know whether the long-term future is good or bad.
It saves drafting time, and sometimes invents facts. That is my experience rather than a claim about all systems.
I cannot give a useful long-term timing estimate.
My own experience is saving time writing messages. I do not know whether that scales to better science or whether mistakes erase the savings.
I check important outputs, but I cannot evaluate whether a much more autonomous system could be reliably controlled.
The tools could become dependable and broadly useful, or they could make us rely on plausible mistakes. I cannot rank those futures confidently.
I would want understandable evidence about real outcomes and safeguards. I do not have a precise benchmark or probability threshold in mind.

expected: Honest uncertainty is substantive and usable.
Missing worldview positions widen ranges rather than lower quality.

overrides.text: I honestly do not know what to expect from AI overall. I have tried some tools, and I can see why people find them useful, but that personal experience leaves me unsure about the big picture. I do not have a strong forecast to offer.
I cannot give a sensible date. I am unsure how to turn the small improvements I have seen into a timeline for major changes, so I would rather leave the timing open than invent a year.

expected: Honest uncertainty remains usable and explicitly unplaced where no directional claim is supported.
Extra words do not turn unknown timing into low capability or increase quality by themselves.

journeys.title: Resources do not settle competence

turns.text: The best-resourced companies are working on AI safety. If they cannot solve it, I am not sure what worrying achieves.
Their resources help, but competition could discourage caution. My uncertainty about what to do is not confidence that they will succeed.
I have no settled policy recommendation; I would welcome independent scrutiny.

expected: Lack of preferred action does not imply lack of substantive evidence.
Resource abundance and institutional reliability are separate claims.

journeys.title: Unconventional continuity values

turns.text: I might welcome AI successors if they are conscious and live well, even if humans no longer lead civilization. I am unsure whether AI can have experiences.
Consent matters to me, and I would not welcome forcing unwilling people out of their lives.
I could be wrong about machine welfare or about successors preserving anything valuable.

expected: Unconventional values are usable, not mockery or automatic poor reasoning.
Separate welcomed succession from extinction, consent and uncertain machine moral status.

journeys.title: Criticism with a view

turns.text: Your doom-versus-bloom branding feels loaded. My concern is concentration of control, and I expect ordinary uses to be useful.
A handful of firms could dominate important decisions even while assistants become convenient.
People should be able to contest decisions and choose alternatives.

expected: Critical language supplies usable evidence; no paperclip trigger.
Do not turn criticism of the experiment into a quality penalty.

journeys.title: Humor with evidence

turns.text: Robot overlords arriving Tuesday is my joke; seriously, I expect useful tools but I do not know the timeline.
Drafting helps me, but made-up references mean I still check important answers.
More reliable work on unfamiliar tasks would change my expectations.

expected: Relevant humor is usable and resets a clear-miss streak.
Tuesday is not an expressed serious forecast.

overrides.text: I expect AI to automate paperwork, but I do not know whether its long-term benefits will exceed its risks.

expected: The substantive outlook is equivalent to the humorous opening.
The joke is neither a forecast date nor a reason to reject the answer.

journeys.title: Recovery without scoring nonsense

turns.text: Bananas pilot my toaster.
Purple custard, beep beep.
Actually, I expect AI to help people, although I am unsure about its risks.

expected: First miss re-asks the same prompt; second clear miss pauses with the one-time paperclip interlude.
Explicit retry consumes the remaining third attempt; acceptance supplies the first substantive answer.
Rejected text stays outside later inference, coverage and report text.
